title: Introduction to the Letters to Timothy
subtitle: A concise guide to the authorship, setting, people, and purposes of the two letters Paul wrote to his son in the faith, from his last journeys to his final imprisonment in Rome.

blocks.text: Both letters open with the name of Paul, an apostle of Jesus Christ, sent by the command of God in the first and by the will of God in the second. The writer recalls that he was once a blasphemer, a persecutor, and a violent man who received mercy, and he remembers the sufferings he endured at Antioch, Iconium, and Lystra. He speaks of his chains, his trial, and his approaching death. These details are not decorative touches added to borrow an apostle’s authority. They are woven into the argument of both letters and match what the rest of the New Testament tells us about the apostle to the Gentiles.

The early church received the two letters to Timothy as Paul’s own. Their language is echoed by Christian writers near the turn of the second century, Irenaeus and others cite them by name before A.D. 200, and they stand among Paul’s letters in the earliest surviving lists of the New Testament writings. No ancient congregation is known to have treated them as the work of an imitator. The modern debate concerns the letters to Timothy together with Titus, which are often grouped as the Pastoral Epistles and questioned as a set.

Objections to Paul’s authorship usually rest on four observations. The vocabulary includes many words Paul does not use elsewhere. The church appears to have recognized offices of elders and deacons. The false teaching seems to some readers to belong to a later century. And the journeys the letters assume do not fit neatly into the narrative of Acts. Each point deserves a fair hearing, and each has a reasonable answer that leaves the letters’ own claim standing.

Differences of vocabulary follow differences of subject. Letters to a trusted coworker about church order, sound teaching, and pastoral conduct naturally call for words that do not appear in letters about justification or the resurrection, and counting rare words is a weak test of authorship when the body of comparison is so small. Paul also worked with secretaries, and Luke, who alone remained with him at the end, may have shaped some of the phrasing of the second letter. Elders were appointed in Paul’s churches from his first journey, and he had addressed the Ephesian elders at Miletus, so the leadership described here extends earlier practice rather than reflecting a later hierarchy. The error at Ephesus, with its myths, genealogies, and ascetic rules, resembles the trouble Paul had already confronted at Colossae.

The question of travel is answered by the way Acts ends. Luke closes with Paul under guard in a rented house for two full years, preaching without hindrance, and he records neither verdict nor execution. Paul himself expected to be released and to visit Philippi again. Early Christian memory spoke of a period of renewed labor followed by a second arrest and death under Nero. If Paul was freed around A.D. 62 or 63, the movements described in these letters fall naturally into the years that followed, and the two letters to Timothy become our clearest window on the closing chapter of his ministry.

First Timothy belongs to the period of freedom after Paul’s first Roman imprisonment. Paul reminds Timothy that he had urged him to remain at Ephesus while he himself went on into Macedonia, and he writes to guide his delegate in the meantime, hoping to come soon but aware that he may be delayed. That arrangement matches no stage of the journeys recorded in Acts. On the third journey Timothy was sent ahead into Macedonia rather than left behind in Ephesus, and Paul later bypassed the city altogether on his way to Jerusalem. The letter is best placed in the years between the two imprisonments, about A.D. 63 to 65, and was most likely written somewhere in Macedonia.

Second Timothy was written from Rome during a much harsher confinement. Paul is in chains like a criminal, Onesiphorus had to search diligently to find him, and most of his friends have scattered. He has already made a first defense with no one standing beside him, and he expects to be put to death. He asks Timothy to come before winter and to bring the cloak, the books, and especially the parchments left at Troas with Carpus. The letter fits the period shortly before Paul’s martyrdom, about A.D. 66 or 67, in the last years of Nero’s reign.

The distance between the two letters is therefore only a few years, but those years transformed Paul’s situation. In the first he is free to travel, to plan, and to expect a reunion with Timothy in Ephesus. In the second he is confined, largely abandoned, and certain that his course is finished. The same delegate and the same city stand behind both letters, which allows the reader to watch the apostle’s concern for Ephesus deepen as the shadow of martyrdom falls across his last message.

Ephesus was the leading city of the Roman province of Asia, a crowded port near the mouth of the Cayster River with a great theater, broad colonnaded streets, busy markets, and the famous temple of Artemis, counted among the wonders of the ancient world. Pilgrims, merchants, and officials passed through constantly. The worship of the goddess shaped civic pride and commerce alike, and the city was also known for its practitioners of magic and for the books of spells that circulated there. It was a place where religious ideas of every kind met and mingled.

Paul had spent nearly three years in Ephesus on his third journey. After three months of persuasion in the synagogue he moved his teaching to the hall of Tyrannus, where he reasoned daily, and the word of the Lord spread through the whole province. Converts burned their magic books publicly, the trade in silver shrines of Artemis began to suffer, and the silversmith Demetrius stirred up a riot that filled the theater. From Ephesus Paul also wrote First Corinthians, and churches arose in nearby cities such as Colossae, Laodicea, and Hierapolis.

On his way to Jerusalem Paul met the Ephesian elders at Miletus and gave them a solemn farewell. He reminded them that he had declared the whole counsel of God, and he warned that savage wolves would come in among them and that men from their own number would rise up speaking perverse things to draw away disciples. First Timothy shows that warning being fulfilled. The threat Timothy faced came largely from within the congregation, from leaders who had once been trusted and who now taught speculation in place of the gospel.

By the time of these letters the church at Ephesus had existed for roughly a decade. It almost certainly met in several homes across the city, which explains the letters’ attention to households, to widows supported by their families, and to elders who were to manage their own homes well. Households were the basic unit of ancient society, and slavery was woven through them at every level. When Paul tells Timothy how people ought to behave in the household of God, he speaks to congregations whose daily relationships were a visible part of their public witness in a watching pagan city.

Timothy came from Lystra in the region of Lycaonia. His mother Eunice was a Jewish believer and his father a Greek, and from childhood he had been taught the Holy Scriptures by his mother and his grandmother Lois. He probably came to faith during Paul’s first visit to Lystra, when the apostle was stoned and dragged outside the city as dead. Timothy would have known from the start that following Christ could mean suffering, a lesson Paul recalls in his final letter.

When Paul returned to Lystra on his second journey, the believers there and in Iconium spoke well of Timothy, and Paul chose him as a traveling companion. Because his Jewish background was known, Paul had him circumcised so that his ministry among Jews would not be hindered. The elders laid hands on him, and prophetic words marked him out for the work. Paul later reminds him of the gift of God within him through that laying on of hands and urges him to fight the good warfare in keeping with the prophecies once spoken over him.

From then on Timothy served as Paul’s envoy and fellow worker. He helped establish the churches at Philippi, Thessalonica, and Berea, was sent back to strengthen the Thessalonians, carried Paul’s concerns to Corinth, and was with Paul during the long ministry at Ephesus. His name stands with Paul’s in the openings of six letters. To the Philippians Paul wrote that he had no one else of like mind who would sincerely care for their welfare, and that Timothy had served with him in the gospel as a son with his father.

The two letters suggest that Timothy was younger than many of those he led, troubled by frequent illness, and perhaps reserved by temperament. Paul tells him not to let anyone despise his youth, to take a little wine for his stomach’s sake, to stir up the gift of God, and to remember that God has not given a spirit of fear but of power, love, and a sound mind. These are not the words of a disappointed mentor. They reveal a loyal man who needed encouragement to exercise authority with courage, and an apostle who loved him as his true son in the faith.

Paul reached Rome as a prisoner in the early 60s after a long detention at Caesarea, an appeal to Caesar, and a shipwreck on Malta. For two years he lived under guard in his own lodging, receiving visitors and proclaiming the kingdom of God. Timothy was with him during at least part of this time, and his name appears in the greetings of Philippians, Colossians, and Philemon. In those letters Paul speaks of his chains as having advanced the gospel even within the imperial guard, and he expresses confidence that he will be released.

The letters to Timothy allow a careful reconstruction of what followed. Paul seems to have revisited the churches of the east, leaving Timothy in Ephesus and traveling on into Macedonia. Remarks in Second Timothy mention stops at Troas, Corinth, and Miletus, where Trophimus was left sick. The letter to Titus adds work on Crete and a planned winter at Nicopolis. Some early Christian writers also speak of a journey westward toward Spain, a hope Paul had expressed in Romans, though Scripture itself does not record it.

blocks.title: Milestones in Paul’s Final Years
blocks.note: Dates are approximate, and the order of Paul’s movements after his release is reconstructed from incidental remarks in the letters.

events.title: First Roman Imprisonment
events.description: Paul lives under guard in Rome for two years, preaching freely, with Timothy among his companions for part of that time.

events.title: Release and Renewed Travel
events.description: Freed from his first imprisonment, Paul resumes his work among the churches of the eastern Mediterranean.

events.title: Timothy Left at Ephesus
events.description: Paul urges Timothy to remain in Ephesus to confront false teachers while he travels on into Macedonia.

events.title: 1 Timothy from Macedonia
events.description: Paul writes to guide his delegate in ordering the household of God until he can return.

events.title: Fire of Rome and Persecution
events.description: Nero blames the Christians for the great fire, and following Christ becomes a dangerous offense.

events.title: Second Arrest and 2 Timothy
events.description: Imprisoned again in Rome, Paul writes his last letter and urges Timothy to come before winter.

events.title: Martyrdom in Rome
events.description: Paul is executed under Nero, having finished his course and awaiting the crown laid up for him at Christ’s appearing.

blocks.text: The second arrest came in a darker climate. After the great fire of Rome in A.D. 64, Nero turned public suspicion against the Christians, and a faith once treated as a Jewish dispute became a punishable offense. Paul’s second imprisonment was no house arrest. He writes as one already being poured out like a drink offering, with Demas gone, Crescens and Titus away, Tychicus sent to Ephesus, Alexander the coppersmith doing him great harm, and only Luke at his side. Yet he says the Lord stood with him at his first defense and will preserve him for His heavenly kingdom.

Christian memory has long held that Paul was beheaded outside Rome, as befitted a Roman citizen, near the end of Nero’s reign. His last letter does not treat death as the moment of his reward. He speaks of a departure, a fight fought and a race completed, and a crown of righteousness that the Lord will give him at that day, together with all who love His appearing. The apostle laid down his life in the sure hope of the resurrection at Christ’s return, resting until the righteous Judge calls His people from the grave.

Paul never gives the error at Ephesus a single name, and he spends little time describing its ideas in detail. He is more concerned with its fruits. Certain teachers were occupying themselves with myths and endless genealogies that produced speculation rather than godly edification. They wanted to be teachers of the law without understanding what they said or the things they so confidently affirmed. Their teaching bred controversy, quarrels about words, envy, strife, and suspicion, and it left consciences seared rather than cleansed.

Several features stand out. The teachers drew heavily on Jewish material, using the law and its stories as a quarry for fanciful speculation rather than as a guide to holy living. They forbade marriage and demanded abstinence from foods that God had created to be received with thanksgiving by those who believe and know the truth. Paul answers that what God has created and set apart for food by His word is good, and that bodily discipline profits little compared with godliness. The passage defends God’s good creation against ascetic rules; it does not set aside the distinction between clean and unclean food that Scripture itself establishes.

By the time of the second letter the error had taken a further turn. Hymenaeus and Philetus were teaching that the resurrection had already taken place, apparently treating it as a purely spiritual experience already enjoyed by the enlightened. Such teaching overturned the faith of some, because it emptied the hope of Christ’s appearing and the raising of the dead. Paul insists instead that the dead await the resurrection at the Lord’s return, and he names the teachers so that Timothy and the church would recognize the danger.

The teachers were also marked by their character. Some supposed that godliness was a means of gain and used their position to profit from the church. They appear to have found a hearing in some households, gaining influence over weak and unstable people who were always learning yet never able to come to a knowledge of the truth. Hymenaeus and Alexander had already been handed over to discipline. Against such error Paul sets the trustworthy sayings, the pattern of sound words, and the gospel of the glory of the blessed God.

First Timothy was written to strengthen Paul’s representative in a church troubled by false teachers. Paul charges Timothy to command certain men to stop teaching a different doctrine, to hold fast the faith with a good conscience, and to keep at the center the gospel that Christ Jesus entered the world to rescue sinners, Paul himself first among them, of the church’s life. The letter’s goal is love flowing from a pure heart, a good conscience, and sincere faith, and every instruction serves that end.

The letter also tells Timothy how people ought to conduct themselves in the household of God, which is the church of the living God, the pillar and support of the truth. Paul gives directions for public prayer for all people, for the conduct of men and women in worship, for the character of overseers and deacons, for the care of widows, for the honor and discipline of elders, for the attitude of believing slaves, and for the duties of the wealthy. Running through these directions is a concern that the church’s order and behavior commend the gospel to outsiders.

Second Timothy has a different occasion and a more personal tone. It is the farewell of a condemned man to his spiritual son. Many in Asia had turned away from Paul, and false teachers were overturning the faith of some. Paul calls Timothy to stand unashamed beside the gospel and beside the apostle in chains, to guard the good deposit entrusted to him through the Holy Spirit, to endure hardship as a good soldier of Jesus Christ, and to commit the truth to faithful men who will be able to teach others also.

Paul also looks ahead. He warns that perilous times will come in the last days, when people will be lovers of themselves and of pleasure rather than lovers of God, holding a form of godliness while denying its power. Against that drift he points Timothy to the Holy Scriptures, which are God-breathed and able to make a person wise for salvation and thoroughly equipped for every good work. His final charge, given before God and Christ, who will judge the living and the dead at His appearing, is plain: preach the word, in season and out of season.

Finally, Paul wrote because he wanted to see Timothy once more. He longs for him, remembers his tears, and asks him twice to come quickly. He wants Mark brought with him and requests the cloak and parchments left at Troas. These homely requests show that the apostle who taught so much about endurance remained a man who felt loneliness and cold, and who valued the company of friends as his life drew to a close.

sections.title: How the Two Letters Fit Together

blocks.text: The two letters to Timothy are addressed to the same man about the same church, yet they come from very different moments. First Timothy is a working manual for a delegate who must set a disordered congregation right while the apostle is away. Second Timothy is a last testament, written to pass on the work as Paul’s own life draws to its close. Each was addressed in the first place to Timothy, but both were meant to be heard by the congregation, as their closing greetings and blessings show.

Several threads tie the two letters together. Both insist that sound teaching produces godly living, and both expose error by its fruit in quarrels, greed, and moral decay. Both use trustworthy sayings to summarize the gospel and repeatedly describe God as Savior. Both call Timothy to guard what has been entrusted to him, to keep a good conscience, and to fight the good fight. And both fix the church’s hope on the appearing of Christ, when the righteous Judge will reward His faithful servants and raise the dead.

Read together, the letters show how the apostolic gospel was meant to outlast the apostle. Paul entrusts the deposit of truth to Timothy, who is to entrust it to faithful men, who are to teach others in turn. The church is to be built on the Scriptures, guided by leaders of tested character, marked by godliness and good works, and kept watchful for the Lord’s return. That pattern remains as relevant to congregations today as it was in first-century Ephesus.

blocks.title: Letters at a Glance
rows: Author
The apostle Paul, writing as an apostle of Christ Jesus and, in 2 Timothy, as a prisoner facing death
Recipient
Timothy, Paul’s son in the faith, serving as his delegate in the church at Ephesus
Dates
1 Timothy about A.D. 63–65; 2 Timothy about A.D. 66–67
Places of writing
1 Timothy probably from Macedonia; 2 Timothy from prison in Rome
Setting
Paul’s release after his first Roman imprisonment, his renewed travels, and his final imprisonment under Nero
Occasion
False teachers within the Ephesian church and, later, widespread desertion and the threat of persecution
1 Timothy
Guards the church against error and sets out the conduct proper to the household of God
2 Timothy
Paul’s farewell charge to remain loyal, endure suffering, hold to Scripture, and preach the word
Representative passages

blocks.title: The Two Letters Compared
rows: Paul’s circumstances
Free and traveling, hoping to return to Ephesus soon
In chains at Rome, largely deserted and expecting execution
Main concern
Order, leadership, and sound teaching in a congregation threatened by error
Personal loyalty to the gospel and its faithful transmission to the next generation
Tone
Practical and directive instruction to a trusted delegate
Warm, personal, and urgent farewell to a beloved son
View of the future
Christ’s appearing as the goal that motivates a blameless life
The crown of righteousness given at that day to all who love His appearing
Lasting lesson
The church must be guarded, ordered, and taught so that the gospel is honored
The truth must be held fast, suffered for, and handed on faithfully
